question: How does Schwab utilize its scale to cheaply acquire new clients and how could Edward Jones replicate a similar strategy?

claims.text: The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) describes Schwab's operating efficiency, 'coupled with scale' and shared infrastructure across businesses, as creating a cost advantage that lets it price competitively while profitably serving clients of various sizes across multiple channels. It also lists brand and reputation as enabling Schwab to attract clients, and service culture as raising the likelihood that clients refer others.
The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) says Schwab was founded to give individual investors access to the markets at a highly competitive cost.

On the 4Q25 earnings call (January 2026), CEO Rick Wurster said Schwab's 'sheer scale, combined with efficiency efforts' keeps cost-to-serve low and lets it invest in client capabilities. He also said that, with nearly $12 trillion in assets and more than 46 million client accounts, doing more for existing clients is as important a growth source as acquiring new clients.

The 2Q26 10-Q (published 2026-08-07) states that management works to couple Schwab's scale and resources with ongoing expense discipline to keep costs low and products affordable. The 10-Q calls this part of its 'no trade-offs' approach.

In the 3Q26 deck (published 2026-10-15), Schwab's 'Keep Cost to Serve Low' page lists a goal to 'leverage our scale to maintain a structural cost advantage while continuing to invest in growth'. The page shows 90% of accounts opened digitally, 82% first call resolution and a 30-second average speed to answer.

Results Schwab cites for 2025: the 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) reports 4.7 million new brokerage accounts (up 13%), core net new assets of $519.4 billion (up 42%, a 5.1% organic growth rate) and 38.5 million active brokerage accounts.

Results Schwab cites for 2026: the 3Q26 press release (2026-10-15) reports 1.2 million new brokerage accounts and $190.4 billion of core net new assets, up 38% versus 3Q25. It also reports 48.6 million total client accounts.

On the 2Q26 call (July 2026), Wurster said Schwab is investing for future client growth in more branches in local communities, more financial consultants, 'strategic marketing and advertising' (including adapting marketing to the influence of LLMs), an RIA support ecosystem and its workplace clients. Per management, acquisition at scale is paired with continued spending, not only low cost.

On the 4Q24 call (January 2025), management said 33% of new-to-firm retail households were under age 30 and more than 50% were under 40. On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), Wurster said 1.9 million new retail households came to Schwab in 2025, and the average new-to-firm retail client is in their 30s.

Workplace: Schwab's investor day deck (published 2026-05-14) says Workplace Services introduces new clients to Retail and Advisor Services. It shows ~400K new-to-firm households introduced by Workplace, ~50% of retirement rollovers retained by Schwab, and ~27% of workplace households using additional Schwab products and solutions.

Workplace: on the 4Q24 call (January 2025), management described a 'multiyear effort to introduce even more workplace clients to our investing and wealth management capabilities'. Schwab's August 2026 monthly report cites 5.9 million workplace plan participant accounts.

Retail: on the 2Q25 call (July 2025), Wurster said clients with a financial consultant relationship bring in more than two times the net new assets, and are more engaged in managed investing and banking, than clients without one. The 10-K (2026-02-25) describes a multichannel service model (online, mobile, phone, branch) and entry products such as Schwab Stock Slices and the Schwab Starter Kit.
Retail digital: Schwab's 3Q26 deck (2026-10-15) shows 90% of accounts opened digitally. The 3Q26 release says Schwab introduced 'Charley', an AI-powered assistant for U.S. retail clients.

Advisor Services: on the 2Q25 call (July 2025), Wurster said Schwab launched Advisor ProDirect, a fee-based, membership-driven offer designed to support independence for new RIAs. On the 4Q25 call (January 2026), he said Schwab attracts net new assets from new and existing advisors of all sizes. The 3Q26 release (2026-10-15) says Schwab partnered with Anthropic to bring Claude for Financial Advisors to the independent RIAs it serves.

Acquisition integration (Ameritrade): on the 4Q24 call (January 2025), management said it captured 100% of the Ameritrade run-rate expense synergies in 2024. On the 2Q25 call (July 2025), Wurster called it the most consequential integration in the industry's history. He said Ameritrade clients moved from losing assets to stable and then growing, and that he expects Ameritrade to become a more meaningful part of net new assets.

Acquisition integration (Forge): the 1Q26 release (2026-04-16) says Schwab closed the Forge Global acquisition in early March 2026. On the 1Q26 call (April 2026), Wurster said Forge will give clients access to pre-IPO shares, to be rolled out over time. He also described a private issuer Equity Services offer that combines the workplace business with Qapita technology and transitions to Schwab's public stock plan services.

Cross-selling: Schwab's investor day deck (published 2026-05-14) lists 'win new clients across Retail, Advisor Services, & Workplace' alongside 'deepen relationships with our existing $12.6T in client assets across 47M accounts'. The 2Q26 release (2026-07-21) cites managed investing net flows up 53%, bank loans of $67.0 billion (up 33%) and Pledged Asset Line balances of $33.4 billion (up 59%).

The 2025 10-K (published 2026-02-25) names its Operating Structure as providing bank, wealth and asset management services to broker-dealer clients, which it says deepens relationships and diversifies revenue.

Edward Jones, 10-K for 2025 (published 2026-03-13): more than 20,000 financial advisors serve more than 9 million clients with $2.5 trillion in client assets under care. The firm has about 55,000 associates and a branch presence in 68% of U.S. counties and all Canadian provinces.

Edward Jones, 2Q25 10-Q (published 2025-08-08): net new assets fell 10% year over year, continuing a downward trend the firm attributes to higher outflows. The firm cites an aging client base, generational wealth transfers outside the firm, macroeconomic volatility, inflation and consumer spending. It had 20,309 financial advisors, and advisor attrition rose to 6.4%, mainly from retirements.

Edward Jones, 3Q25 10-Q (published 2025-11-07): net new households were 24,000 in the quarter versus 53,000 a year earlier (-55%), and 101,000 for the nine months versus 177,000 (-43%). Client households were 6.7 million (up 3%) and financial advisors at period end were 20,429 (up 3%).

Edward Jones, 1Q26 10-Q (published 2026-05-07): client households were 6.8 million at period end versus 6.6 million (up 3%), and net new assets were $18 billion versus $17 billion. Operating expenses rose 13% to $4,136 million, against net revenue up 12% to $4,677 million. The firm cites higher financial advisor compensation, variable compensation and communications and data processing from 'continued investments in new tools and technology'. Income before allocations margin was 11.5%.

Edward Jones, 2Q26 10-Q (published 2026-08-07): first-half 2026 net new assets rose 6% and operating expenses rose 15% to $8,533 million. Income before allocations margin was 11.7% for the first half, which the firm describes as 'a strategic balance between investing in the future and current financial results'.

Edward Jones, 10-K for 2025 (published 2026-03-13), competition and recruiting: the firm names competition from discount firms 'usually with lower levels of personalized service', including major brokerage firms with zero commissions, plus robo-advice and fintechs. It also names 'intense competition among firms to attract and retain qualified professionals, including financial advisors'.

Edward Jones, 10-K for 2025 (published 2026-03-13), new-client initiatives: the Partnership is 'making substantial investments' in initiatives that include High Net Worth, Workplace (local business owners and their employees) and a new digital platform for Next Generation investors. The 10-K says their success depends on broad adoption by financial advisors, CSTPs and home office associates, and that the firm cannot reliably predict timing or outcome.

Edward Jones, 2025 10-Qs, 'Enterprise Reimagined': the firm describes a multi-tiered initiative to restructure and reduce the size of the home office, remove redundancies and adopt new capabilities, processes and technology. It says this will create more efficient operations, and it cites estimated separation costs in expenses.

Edward Jones, strategic priorities in its own words (10-K for 2025, published 2026-03-13): the strategic ambition is to help 'tens of millions of investors' achieve financial fulfillment. The firm aspires to continue investing in technology to scale its ability to provide financial planning, anticipate clients' needs with the right offering at the right time, and attract and serve new client segments.

Edward Jones, technology and digital (10-K for 2025): the firm says industry competition is driving 'significant investments' in financial advisors, technology infrastructure, digital initiatives, knowledge- and data-powered tools and strategic relationships. It lists a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.

Edward Jones, technology spending (10-Qs for 1Q26 and 2Q26, published 2026-05-07 and 2026-08-07): the firm attributes higher communications and data processing expense to continued investments in new tools and technology and related higher depreciation.

Edward Jones, workplace and retirement channel (trade press, WealthManagement.com, 2026-09-30; indicative only): the firm is developing an end-to-end retirement plan management platform with Aboon and Retirement Plan Advisory Group, to be integrated into the advisor workstation. The prospecting module is in beta with advisors and is expected to reach the broader network early next year. The article says Edward Jones advisors serve over 263,000 workplace retirement plans with nearly $107 billion in assets under care and more than 1.3 million plan participants. It also says about two-thirds of U.S. advisors have a group retirement plan client.

Edward Jones, banking (10-K for 2025, published 2026-03-13): the Utah and FDIC conditionally approved the application for Edward Jones Bank in February 2026, and the Partnership expects to open it by early 2027. For comparison, Schwab's 2025 10-K lists bank, wealth and asset management services within its operating structure.

Edward Jones, planning technology (trade press, InvestmentNews/Kitces, 2026-08-18; indicative only): the firm took a minority stake in Quicken. The article says Edward Jones intends to integrate Quicken's personal financial management capabilities, but is still determining the deployment strategy.

Schwab comparison points on the same dimensions: Schwab's 3Q26 deck (2026-10-15) shows 90% of accounts opened digitally. Its investor day deck (published 2026-05-14) shows ~400K new-to-firm households introduced by Workplace. Schwab's 2025 10-K reports 4.7 million new brokerage accounts. Edward Jones's 3Q25 10-Q reports 101,000 net new households for the first nine months of 2025.

The evidence above only provides objective context for the strategic question asked. Whether or how Edward Jones should act is a judgment for the strategy team to make, beyond the scope of this evidence engine.

adjacent.text: Trade press (InvestmentNews, 2026-11-12): a financial advisor who managed approximately $185 million at Edward Jones left to launch an independent practice on LPL's platform. The article cites ISS Market Intelligence data that LPL recorded more than 7,200 net advisor additions over the five years ending in 2025.
adjacent.differs_because: Trade-press reporting is indicative, not authoritative. It describes one advisor departure and LPL's recruiting, not Edward Jones's attrition or recruiting costs.

gaps.what: Schwab: a cost-per-acquired-client or marketing spend per new account is not disclosed in the evidence provided. The 'low cost' claim rests on management's statements about scale and cost-to-serve, not a measured acquisition cost.
gaps.suggested_source: Schwab investor day materials or 10-K expense detail on advertising and promotional spend, plus any management disclosure of acquisition cost per account

gaps.what: Edward Jones: client acquisition cost, marketing and advertising spend, and digital lead-generation results are not found in the evidence provided.
gaps.suggested_source: Edward Jones 10-K expense detail and management commentary on marketing, branding and new-client sourcing

gaps.what: Edward Jones: the cost and productivity of recruiting and training new financial advisors are not found in the evidence provided. Only advisor counts, attrition and aggregate expense growth are covered.
gaps.suggested_source: Edward Jones 10-K or investor materials on advisor recruiting, training investment and new-advisor productivity

gaps.what: Edward Jones: a low-cost or no-fee digital offering and any stated plan for centralized or scale-based cost-to-serve are not found in the evidence provided. The 10-K names a new digital platform for Next Generation investors, but gives no pricing or scale-economics detail.
gaps.suggested_source: Edward Jones management commentary, investor materials or product pages on the Next Generation digital platform and pricing
